newsitem.title: UK: Bank of England piles on pressure for higher rates.
newsitem.headline: Bank of England piles on pressure for higher rates.

text.p: The Bank of England shocked UK markets with an aggressive line on inflation in its quarterly report and analysts said it will probably win its battle to see higher interest rates in the months ahead.

"It seems to be a fairly clear call for further rate rises," said Nigel Richardson, head of bond research at Yamaichi International. "I think rates will go up before the election. There will certainly be one rise, possibly two."
In its quarterly inflation report, the Bank said a further rate increase was likely to be needed in due course if the government was to meet its 2.5 percent inflation target.

And given that Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke sanctioned a surprise quarter-point rate rise last week even though elections are due by May 1997, he may not stand in the way of further policy tightening.
"If he was convinced by the merits of a quarter-point rise previously, if there was enough concern there, he will be willing to go along with a further rise," Richardson said.

The Bank's report said even after base rates were raised to 6.0 percent last week, there is now much less chance of underlying inflation being below 2.5 percent during 1997, than was the case three months ago.
And in a departure from other inflation reports this year, the Bank also highlighted the short-term risks to inflation.
Bank chief economist Mervyn King said it was possible inflation would jump above 3.0 percent in the next month or so. RPIX inflation stood at 2.9 percent year-on-year in September.
"The BoE is going for the jugular by talking up inflation concerns," said Ian Gunner, economist at Chase Investment Bank.
He said the fact that British building societies had not raised mortgage rates after last week's official rate rise, made another monetary tightening before the election more likely.
Domestic consumer demand is driving economic growth in the UK and until borrowing rates, on houses and other areas rise, high street spending is unlikely to abate, analysts said.
Bank chief economist Mervyn King denied that was the case, saying perceptions about borrowing rates would have been shifted by last week's move, even if home loan rates were not.
The Bank also rejected any ideas that a stronger pound was any substitute for higher interest rates.
So it is unlikely to accept the currency argument for leaving interest rates on hold even though its report said the stronger pound had no medium-term implications for UK inflation.
"The last rate hike came against a background of a sharp rise in sterling and that wasn't sufficient to quell it so I don't think the recent rise does either," Richardon said.
In any case, the Bank said it expected sterling's rally -- it is up almost nine percent on a trade-weighted basis since early August -- to peter out at some point.
The report said the perception of rising rates in Britain coupled with lower rates abroad, would probably prove temporary.
The foreign exchanges took the Bank at its word and the pound dropped two pfennigs from its early morning high.
Some analysts said the Bank may be going over the top about inflation in order to ensure the mistakes of the 1980s, which led to a boom/bust cycle, are not repeated.

"The Bank is being so pessimistic because the UK is at a stage in the economic cycle where mistakes can easily be made," said Kevin Adams, gilts analyst at BZW. "It is anxious that the good is not undone. "They are overegging things a wee bit."
But whatever its motives, the hawkishness of the Bank's tone could not be ignored.

"The surprise is that the Bank are being more aggressive than expected," Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said on Reuters Financial Television. "The Bank is tightening the screws."
